cells.tense: Right now you're the one shaping this ending — not waiting on it, and not caught under it.
cells.ask: Offer one ending past the point that feels tidy — tonight, say out loud that something is over instead of letting it trail, and watch how the next morning sits.
cells.core:
You're the one who decides where this ends, and you do it in a way people can lean on. You draw the line, you say what's done, and the wobbling stops — there's solid ground under the next thing because you laid it. The people around you feel that floor, and the endings you name hold long enough for what comes after to take its first real step. This is the seat working the way it's built to work, and it's working here.

The ending you keep putting off, you can put it down early for once. Say the thing is finished before enough time has passed to make it official, and let how plain that is do something for whoever's been waiting to hear it.

cells.tense: Somewhere in you the ending is already finished, and you're living on the far side of a room that hasn't emptied yet.
cells.ask: Take the ending you've thought through most and leave one thing about it unwritten today — one detail of what comes after stays blank until tomorrow.
cells.core:
You're sorting this ending ahead of schedule. The order you make is real and it holds, but you're tidying a room the change hasn't reached, so the next thing gets decided before it's had a chance to show you what it is. That's the tax on arriving early — the part that only shows up in the middle of the thing doesn't get to show up for you.

Let one piece of what comes after stay unplanned for a day. What you can already see will still be there without being nailed down in advance, and whatever turns up in the gap is yours to meet.

cells.tense: You're standing in front of a door that closed behind you a while back, still holding the pieces of something that ended without anyone saying so.
cells.ask: At the table you're at, write down the three things stacked on you and put one line through the one that isn't getting done — just the line, today.
cells.core:
There's a shelf in you where everything goes and nothing gets sorted. Pieces pile up, promises pile up, and the ending that would clear the air keeps not getting named — so you carry all of it at once and very little gets finished. It isn't that you can't organize. One ending has to be said out loud before the rest can fall into line.

Name the one thing that's actually over — out loud or on paper, it's the same size — and let clearing that make room for starting. You don't have to feel finished first. Saying so is what finishes it.

cells.tense: There's a structure running through this stretch and you keep calling yourself messy, but the pen is already in your hand.
cells.ask: Tell one person you're the one holding this ending together — say it plainly, once, and let it be yours.
cells.core:
People around you are standing on something you've quietly built. The order holds because you keep making it hold, and you haven't named that as yours, so the building stays invisible and you feel behind on a plan that's already running. The shape is there. Only the naming of it is missing.

When the next ending comes, say it as the one who decided it — to yourself first, if that's easier than saying it to them. Being the one who chose won't make the ending heavier. It just stops the work from happening off to the side, where you don't get to count it.

attempts.check: The cells know the card, the seat and the status — not the person — so the Too Much and Too Little cells must never plant a history (a past failure, a person who reacted badly, years of habit); they can say where the person is standing in time, not what happened there. A reader might reasonably say 'I'm not in charge of anything here' or 'my mess is real, not hidden' — both are answerable, since the ask is one visible act a camera could see, not a verdict on their whole situation, and the experiment still teaches them something if the reading's wrong about them. The sentence I cut as serving the writer more than the reader: an early line that declared 'you are the author of the ending' — it echoed the house's own vocabulary about authorship rather than anything the person would hear across a table.
